column2: The São Paulo exhibition organized by MoMA shows his figurative and abstract canvases of 1947-52; in 1952 he is shown at the Carnegie Institute's Pittsburgh International (again in 1955, 1958, 1961, 1964, and 1970).

Chaet, furious, reports to Albers that Keller told students who had come to see the Cézanne exhibition at the Met that Cézanne was the greatest faker in history; Albers finds it hilarious and calms Chaet down. Consequences: Albers's strategy: ignore the old guard, never call faculty meetings

Thanks to the American High Commissioner in Germany, John McCloy, won over by the energy and determination of Inge Scholl (met during a visit to Boston in January 1950), the school receives DM 1,000,000 ($250,000) in funding from the American government. Sum: DM 1,000,000 ($250,000) Consequences: Scholl's dream comes true

Promised as early as 1950, the funding of DM 1,000,000 ($250,000) through the American High Commissioner is released only in 1952, after the political neutrality of the future HfG has been verified. DM 1,000,000 ($250,000) Consequences: Inge Aicher-Scholl's dream comes true.

Anticipating the retirement of Howe (then laid up in Philadelphia with one of his colds), Sawyer writes in confidence to Schweikher, a Yale alumnus and Chicago architect, inviting him to be the future chairman of the Department of Architecture. Howe laid up in Philadelphia with one of his bouts of colds; Gene Nalle shares the concern

Janis, Albers's dealer since his gallery opened in 1948 (and into the 1970s), begins showing de Kooning and his circle, soon collectively called the “Abstract Expressionists.” Consequences: Albers fears that his students will ape these painterly abstractions and leads a vocal, outraged crusade against the Schmierkunst of the New York School

A ceramics seminar welcoming the British potter Bernard Leach, the Bauhaus potter Marguerite Wildenhain, the Japanese curator and historian Soetsu Yanagi, and Shoji Hamada, a potter who will later become a Living National Treasure of Japan. Four international guests in ceramics

During the 1952 summer session, Shahn asks his audience for whom one paints, and later answers that the public function of art has always been to create community; that is not necessarily its intention, but it is its result. Consequences: Formulates the link between art and community characteristic of BMC

In a 1952 document (a prospectus for the spring semester, February 11–June 7, 1952), Olson writes that what one must look for is not things in themselves but what happens between things. He fondly quotes William Carlos Williams's formula “no ideas but in things”. Semester from February 11 to June 7, 1952

The first composition made exclusively of meticulously cut and spliced magnetic tape, ranging from mechanical noise to recorded music; the score is a nearly illegible drawing on graph paper in which the squares correspond to durations. The title pays tribute to the financial support of Paul and Vera Williams, regulars at the college. Marker on paper, 8.5 × 11 inches for the score Consequences: Leads Cage to his lifelong use of chance procedures

The summer he is working on the piece, Cage makes it the subject of a class, but the students, too clever, do not show up, knowing that taking part would mean hours of painful cutting and splicing of magnetic tape.

Cage assigns each performer time brackets during which he or she can do anything at all: the principle of collage carried over into performance. Memories are hazy, especially about Olson's presence. Rauschenberg may have played Édith Piaf records; some remember one of his White Paintings hanging from the ceiling. Édith Piaf records, a White Painting hanging from the ceiling Consequences: A founding moment of the happening; after this summer, Rauschenberg leaves for New York
During the summer of 1952, Rauschenberg takes Cunningham's dance classes, just as Cage returns there; all of it documented by the photography teacher Hazel Larsen Archer.

A spring 1952 bulletin asserts that the college's central effort is to teach method and not content, process rather than facts. Black Mountain College Bulletin 9, no. 4 (Spring 1952). Consequences: Shows that the Alberses' legacy persisted until 1952.

A college bulletin proclaims that the central effort is to teach method, not content, and to emphasize process; Molesworth sees in it the lasting legacy of the Alberses and their concern with the formal and the haptic. Quotation: “Our central and consistent effort is to teach method, not content…” Consequences: The Alberses' teaching legacy persists after their departure.
In early 1952, Olson invites Wildenhain to serve as official host of the seminar, Karnes and Weinrib not yet having been hired.
According to Mary Emma Harris, a series of administrative reorganizations and failed fund-raising campaigns strikes the college from 1952 on, one of its darkest periods.

Plan of the room (drawn by M.C. Richards for William Fetterman in 1989): the audience seated in squares in the center, Cunningham dancing along a path between the spectators, Tudor's piano, Cage reading on a ladder, Rauschenberg's phonograph, Kline's hanging painting, the entrance near the dining hall. Ladder, phonograph, paper handed to the performers.
According to Mary Emma Harris, a series of administrative reorganizations and failed attempts at fund-raising begins in 1952 and plunges the college into one of its darkest periods.

Kline teaches in the summer of 1952 and goes on developing there his opaque black-and-white compositions, a structural abstraction free of expression (Wotan 1950, Painting No. 11 1951, Untitled 1952). Photograph of Kline with Painting at Black Mountain, the canvas nailed above a door against the side of a white clapboard house (photograph by William Douglas McGee)

A less famous event of the summer of 1952: Hermine, daughter of Jack Tworkov, who teaches painting, receives presents made by Rauschenberg and Dorothea Rockburne. Rauschenberg makes the photogram Untitled (a birthday picture for Hermine)

Rauschenberg photographs the Tworkov girls: one picture shows them huddled in a clump of ferns; in the other, Hermine in profile in front of a tapestry of trees and grasses, her hair loosely tied, her body slumped. He uses a shallow depth of field to flatten the space between the foliage and the girl, accentuating the sharp outline of her silhouette, in natural light.

Nicholas Cernovich prints Duncan's poem as a broadside in the spring of 1952, with a linocut cover attributed to Cy Twombly but probably made in collaboration with Rauschenberg, in the intense months after Rauschenberg's separation from Susan Weil. Printed in red ink on laid paper, with a coral wrapper; sheet 20 x 13½ inches, accompanied by the poem on a separate sheet and a typed manuscript. Consequences: A legendary object among BMC art books.
After taking part in BMC's Pottery Seminar in the fall of 1952, Wildenhain declines the offer to join the faculty and goes back to live at Pond Farm until her death in 1985.
At Yale in 1952, Anni Albers takes the art historian George Kubler's course on Mesoamerican art, one of the sources of On Weaving. Consequences: Directs her interest toward ancient textiles.
A wire sculpture nearly ten feet tall intrigues the public and swings like a clock pendulum when visitors pass by. Nearly 3 m tall, in wire

Just before the sculpture is sent to New York, Cunningham photographs Untitled (S.535) at her home in unusual positions: rolled up on itself on the floor, printed in negative. A photograph titled “Aiko with Mobile” is submitted to the San Francisco Women Artists annual, with color portraits of Asawa holding the work. Unusual positions, negative print, the title “Aiko with Mobile” Consequences: Places Asawa's work in the category of the mobile, and thus of contemporary sculpture.

The curator Edgar Kaufmann asks Asawa for examples of her baskets for his Good Design exhibitions; he defines “good design” as a response to the needs of a new public of free individuals in an industrialized world. Little room is left in it for the artist-mother working at home. A request for baskets for the 1952 edition Consequences: Asawa's reception in the design circuit, brief according to the author.
Back in North Carolina in the spring; he spends the summer painting at the college and reconnects with Cage, Cunningham, Fuller, Tworkov, Motherwell, and Kline.
Leaves for Europe in the fall; the two travel together in Italy, France, and Spain.

Steichen, sensing the young artist's potential, acquires two black-and-white photographs for his institution: the first works by Rauschenberg to enter a public collection. Two black-and-white prints (pl. 1 and 26), the only vintage prints in existence Consequences: First work in a public collection

Rauschenberg photographs his friends at Black Mountain: John Cage in his Model A Ford (the very car that will be used for Automobile Tire Print the following year) and Franz Kline; some photographs are by Twombly, others by Rauschenberg, others cannot be attributed; the camera is known to have belonged to Rauschenberg Cage's Model A Ford; Rauschenberg's camera; uncertain attribution of the pictures Consequences: A testament to the collaborative relationship between Rauschenberg and Twombly

For Twombly's grant application, Rauschenberg photographs his friend's paintings, in fact large, carefully dry-mounted enlargements Large enlargements, dry mounting Consequences: The grant they obtain makes the joint trip possible

The two artists visit and photograph the sites, stroll through the Porta Portese market, and buy knickknacks and souvenirs; Rauschenberg photographs the objects in the market: torn fabrics, tarpaulins over rusty objects, old-fashioned mannequins, neglected paintings Torn fabrics, tarpaulins, mannequins, unloved canvases Consequences: These images resonate with the Surrealist aesthetic of the found object (Breton, Mad Love)
Just after leaving BMC in 1952, he travels in Europe: first a welcome obscurity, then a blinding exposure to the spotlight in Venice. Consequences: The opening of his international career
Just after leaving BMC in 1952, he begins eye-opening travels in Europe; he had earlier known Paris briefly and feverishly as a novice, fifteen years too late, he says with regret

Cage, Cunningham, the pianist Tudor, and the poet Olson collaborate; Rauschenberg presents a slide show and hangs his modular white paintings as a backdrop. The first American attempt at a theatrical synthesis of the arts. White Paintings used as a set; slide show by Rauschenberg Consequences: A prototype of the “Happenings” (Kaprow, Oldenburg, Dine, New York, 1959), which will pave the way for Pop Art

In the summer of 1952, Rauschenberg takes part in John Cage's untitled event at Black Mountain College, considered the American precedent of mixed-media theater. Consequences: The precedent of the happening in America

Edward Steichen acquires two photographs taken at Black Mountain College, Untitled (Interior of an Old Carriage) (1949) and Untitled (Cy on Bench) (1951): the first works by Rauschenberg to enter a museum. Two BMC photographs

Cage composes his silent piece in response to the White Paintings; the score specifies three parts (original durations 33", 2'40", and 1'20"), performable by any instrument and of any length. The same year: Cage at the college, where the work was performed. Handwritten score: three parts of 33", 2'40", and 1'20"; the durations given, the piano lid closed at the beginnings and opened at the ends; any instrument, any length Consequences: Founds Cage's aesthetic of silence, saturated with ever-present sound

The handwritten score names Tudor as the pianist of the premiere, with the beginnings and ends of the parts marked by closing and opening the keyboard lid. The pianist's gestures: closing the keyboard lid to begin, opening it to end

Cage composes 4'33", a work in three tacet parts; the reproduced manuscript specifies that the beginnings are signaled by closing the piano's keyboard lid and the ends by opening it, that the work may be performed on any instrument or combination of instrumentalists and at any length, and that it was performed by the pianist David Tudor. On the manuscript dated the 29th (month illegible) 1952: three parts of 32", 2'40", and 1'20"; keyboard lid closed to begin, opened to end; free instrumentation. Consequences: The work becomes a transmissible concept, preparing the performance instructions of Fluxus and Conceptual art.
Cage's second event at the college: a use of chance processes, later proclaimed the first “Happening,” with a “purpose to remove purposes.” Consequences: The founding act of the Happening

Devised by Cage and David Tudor: multiple participants in overlapping time segments for a total of 45 minutes. Olson and M.C. Richards read their poetry, Rauschenberg shows his paintings and plays records, Cunningham dances, Tudor plays the piano, Cage reads a prepared lecture on Zen Buddhism. Added to this are slides projected upside down onto tilted surfaces (a cross-shaped arrangement of Rauschenberg's White Paintings). Chairs in a concentric arrangement, a square made of four triangles converging toward the center without meeting, allowing the performers to move through the audience. 45 minutes; White Paintings in a cross; upside-down slides; chairs in four triangles Consequences: Inaugurates the dispersal of attention and the radical fragmentation of narrative; with no rehearsals and no set script

A two-week seminar announced by a calligraphed card: a black wash cut into graphic panels with sketches of pots, lists of discussions, demonstrations, and speakers. Themes: the development of ideas of form, design for mass production, craft in the world of the machine, teaching (master and apprentice: in the workshop, at college), the relation between craft and art. Wildenhain as “host potter,” Leach and Hamada give demonstrations, Yanagi lectures on Buddhist aesthetics. Flyer: “eastern center for interchange of work & ideas east to west,” September 22 to November 15, address: Registrar, Black Mountain College, North Carolina; Hamada introduced simply as “the Japanese potter,” director of the Imperial Folk Museum. Consequences: A catalyzing event for postwar American ceramics; Wildenhain's Pottery: Form and Expression grows out of it.

After the Dartington Hall conference in the summer of 1952, the three men tour the United States: Black Mountain College, California, the Archie Bray Foundation (Montana), where Voulkos meets Hamada for the first time. Consequences: The spread of Japanese folk-craft ideas in America.

A crafts conference initiated by Bernard Leach at the experimental English college founded by Dorothy and Leonard Elmhirst; the speakers include many of Leach's friends and disciples (Yanagi, Hamada, Cardew, Heron), with the notable exception of Marguerite Wildenhain, invited on the theme “The Potter in the New World.” Consequences: Black Mountain's ceramics seminar in the fall of 1952 takes up part of it.

A tour passing through Black Mountain College, California, and the Archie Bray Foundation in Montana, where Peter Voulkos meets Hamada for the first time. Consequences: A decisive encounter for Voulkos.

A ceramics seminar in the fall of 1952, taking up part of the Dartington conference. Leach at first refuses to demonstrate, arguing that he does not know the materials available, and agrees only to lecture; under pressure he gives in. Hamada, by contrast, says he can make do with what he finds: clays and glazes gathered on the hillside in front of the workshop, weed stalks tied in a bundle to serve as improvised brushes. Clay and glazes from the hillside, improvised brushes of weed stalks. Consequences: For the audience of potters and students, seeing Hamada use the wheel not as an exercise in perfect form but as a starting point for other manipulations revealed how academic American pottery had become.

A collection self-published by Jonathan Williams: verses by Williams, drawings and statements by Paul Ellsworth, a large folded sheet mounted in boards covered with Japanese paper, with a photograph of Williams pasted on the front board. Small 4to, 4 drawings by Ellsworth, Japanese paper
Broadside No. 1 of the Black Mountain College Graphics Workshop, text by Charles Olson, cover by Nicholas Cernovich.

Fall 1952, after the Kline/Tworkov summer. An afternoon with a fake gin bottle (filled with water): feigned drunkenness, two glasses, sun through the window, a view across the hall to the light on the mountain, dust motes, an exchange of blue jeans and T-shirts, until the dinner gong from the other shore; headaches on the road. Nights in a rowboat on the lake: home brew in Mason jars, songs, kisses, the croaking of frogs, crickets, night birds, bats, the mountain rising like a bass crash; back at dawn, parting on the steps of North Lodge. She poses for his drawings; he then falls for a beautiful sixteen-year-old Jewish girl who came into his arms at a dance. After the breakup: an understanding of Mondrian (“early work”) in a final separation, in admiration. A gin bottle filled with water; Mason jars; the dinner gong; a rowboat; Philip Guston, enthusiastic, invites him to New York to see his work; back home, in the dime store, a girl cries “You look like Jesus!” when he lets his beard grow; letter: “You are the artist… none without the other” Consequences: She leaves on her motorcycle and goes on with science; JoAnne Cunningham, the girl from the dime store, will later run off to Cuba with a lover

Dawson curses those who sawed these posts by machine without having to work them; Dan brings up the tractor and wonders what an oak knot does to the teeth of a power saw, then smiles: “Technology creeps on”. Consequences: A little tension between them

Coming home exhausted, they run into Doyle in his garden. Forced politeness, then Doyle laughs loudly and slaps Dawson on the back: “You're damned RIGHT you will”, “That's OAK!”, “That oak is gonna teach you”. His eyes flash at the word “teach”; Dan frowns: “He sure has it bad.” Repeated laughter, a slap on the back Consequences: The end of a working friendship: months of 15-hour days side by side at the silos, then the affectionate “goodnight,” Claire's coffee or home brew, all of it dead because of Doyle's hostility toward Olson; Dawson becomes suspect

Absorbed in nailing face to face, each on his own nail, they do not see night fall. Dawson notices that his nail has changed color (lead and violet), then realizes it is dark. “Let's quit! For Christ's sake — it's NIGHT!” Dan: “Well by God, so it is.” “Beautiful.” “It is.” A nail turned lead-gray and violet in the darkness

Once, exasperation boils over: Dawson insists the saw was at the corner of the foundation yesterday; Dan denies it, gets angry, red in the face, then runs off stepping over the debris, picks up the saw somewhere else, and brandishes it: “Here — HERE is your saw!”

From 150 feet below, against the tree line and the late afternoon sky: straight posts, middle beams, flat boards on top, a classic form. Dawson has driven half the nails and knows every one. Dan mutters bitterly: “Now those fatheads can come up and ruin it.” Consequences: Others do in fact add crossbeams, braces, two hundred more nails, and a roof like an upturned Viking ship, claiming the structure would not hold

Dissatisfied with Woman I after eighteen months, he stops working on it; Meyer Schapiro sees the work a few months later and helps him find a way to finish it; he spends the summer at the Castellis' while continuing Woman I. Eighteen months of work.

When Cage takes the path of chance and then of indeterminacy in 1952, his friendship with Albers breaks down: Albers cannot bear the implications Cage now carries and feels that Cage is renouncing his responsibility as an artist. Quotation from Cage: “our friendship was broken... he felt that I was renouncing my responsibility as an artist” Consequences: An irreducible conflict between two visions of testing and contingency in art

Composed during his stay, after ripening for several years; the three sections (33 seconds, 2 min 40 s, 1 min 20 s) are determined by the I Ching. Durations: 0:33 / 2:40 / 1:20 Consequences: Premiered by Tudor in 1952 (a premiere described with the sheets set on the piano, the lid closed at each section, a stopwatch consulted)

One evening, Cage and others read the whole of Huang Po's Doctrine of Universal Mind with all the notes; participants will later tell him that their lives had changed. A one-evening reading, a ninth-century text Consequences: A central inspiration for the new directions of his work at Black Mountain

M.C. Richards, a faculty member, translates the major texts of Antonin Artaud, later collected under the title The Theater and Its Double. Consequences: This translation indirectly shapes Cage's Theater Piece No. 1.

Throughout the summer of 1952, Cage, Tudor, and Richards discuss Artaud intensely at the college and closely study chapters of The Theater and Its Double as a counterpart to the theses on emptiness and the elimination of intention (Cage's doctrine). Consequences: The direct matrix of Theater Piece No. 1.
Cage apparently tried to reproduce Duchamp's experiment: dropping a one-meter thread three times and recording the shapes obtained. A one-meter thread dropped three times.

Cage declares that he would not be satisfied with that kind of chance operation in his work: he likes details and wants things more complicated. Erratum Musical: 25 notes drawn from a hat by Duchamp and his two sisters, from the F below middle C to the high F.

The students refuse to sign up for his summer class, whose stated aim was to recruit helpers to cut and splice tape for Williams Mix; Cage then cancels all formal teaching for the session. The tedious work of cutting and splicing bits of magnetic tape for the composition Williams Mix Consequences: His stay at BMC remains associated with performances rather than teaching

Fuller writes that it is historically easy for insurgent politicians to stir up the 99% of have-nots against the few privileged men, a rhetoric the author compares to contemporary far-right commentators. Fuller gives up mass political action, which he calls mass populism or a “mob outburst.”

Díaz notes that in 1952 Albers was already exhibiting Homage to the Square and working on the Structural Constellations; he proposes 1947–50 as the best dating of the Variants series. A Variant reproduced from a 2003 PaceWildenstein catalog dated 1947–55.
Events started at the time for fun (later for charity); Elaine, memorable at the plate, hit home runs by any means, especially by cheating.
Exhibition of Fuller's geodesic dome at MoMA, the occasion for Elaine de Kooning's article “Dymaxion Artist.” Consequences: An article by Elaine de Kooning

Rosenberg publishes in Art News the definition and name of the American movement henceforth called Action Painting. Art News, 1952. Consequences: The movement receives a published label and definition.

Four cars arrive; the host locks the Scotch, gin, and vodka in a cabinet, planning a dinner with Moselle; he goes out to check the kitchen; Kline pries open the cabinet and passes the bottles around Atmosphere: a comedy of alcoholic sedition in the countryside Stakes: a collision of two cultures of conviviality, German and New York

Arrival in four cars; the artists unpack Scotch, gin, and vodka; Hensler locks up the liquor and serves his Moselle; as soon as he goes to check on the kitchen, Kline forces the cabinet and passes the bottles around; the leg of lamb is devoured amid a Cedar Tavern uproar; at dawn, the war over the beds is not settled; Elaine, in her cast, announces that she is walking back to New York and limps off; Bill goes after her; everyone leaves Words: Elaine: he wanted a philosophical discussion, but they were all drinking martinis, and the more pompous Fritz became, the wilder they got; Abel: they seemed to have come to New Jersey just to prove they had never left Eighth Street and University Place Atmosphere: Drinking by moonlight, snickering, a damp dawn Stakes: The clash between the European culture of the dinner party and the joyful wildness of the New York School; the de Koonings' little theater

Every day, a trek to the swimming hole because the lake is polluted; after swimming, everyone sits on the bank choosing and admiring the smooth pebbles Atmosphere: summer intimacy, with Rauschenberg's immense future in the background

A cool, misty fall morning; Dawson, sitting on the rocks, hears a muffled rustling; Dehn appears, hollow-cheeked but rosy, eyes bright, white hair in the wind, collar up, a little stooped; smiles exchanged, a murmured hello; the small figure passes and disappears into the fog. Words: a murmured “hello” Atmosphere: mist, silence, twilight gentleness: a farewell without knowing it Stakes: the old scholar is fading away; paradise is closing for Dawson too, soon to be drafted

Olson reads the three stories that won the Barnard prize, rises from his chair, and shouts his verdict and his ban on publishing for ten years Words: “You're still writing conservative junk!”; “AND ABOVE ALL DON'T TRY TO PUBLISH ANYTHING FOR TEN YEARS!” Atmosphere: the fury of the six-foot-seven giant towering over the student Stakes: a repetition of the censoring father; a swing from glory to disgrace

At the end of the summer, Olson suggests that McGee stay; McGee makes his staying conditional on a master's degree; Olson rubs his chin, sizes him up with his enormous eyes, and calls the board together, which deliberates for a morning before giving up Words: “Okay, I'm going to call a meeting of the Board of Fellows to see if this can be worked out” Atmosphere: the comic seriousness of the deliberation, the generosity of the effort Stakes: the institutional improvisation of a college running out of breath

The first face seen on arrival: Rauschenberg immediately offers a hand unloading the '39 Ford, spots the small canvases covered with zinc white, holds one at arm's length, and is enthusiastic about what was meant to be mere recycling Words: “What's this!… This is really an interesting painting” Atmosphere: a warm welcome, the young painter's bewilderment Stakes: genius reveals beauty where the student saw only a canvas to reuse

Night; Adams, stuck on his own canvas, goes to knock at Rauschenberg's door; Rauschenberg turns on the porch light; Adams sees his shoeprints on the canvas laid out to dry; Rauschenberg stares at him intently and calmly asks whether he was wearing interesting shoes; the prints become part of the painting Words: “My God, Bob! I'm afraid I've ruined your painting!” — “Did you have on interesting shoes?” Atmosphere: The dark porch, sudden light, horror, then comic calm Stakes: An emblem of the avant-garde at BMC: the accident becomes the work

Late at night, Cage reads the whole of Huang Po (notes and preface included) before 20-30 people; several assist him, acting out the dialogue in which the master insults the pupil. Atmosphere: Nocturnal solemnity; a profound effect on a Korean War veteran at the end of his rope. Stakes: Cage's only formal teaching that summer.

8:30 p.m. according to Francine du Plessix (a planned length of 45 minutes, though the accounts stretch over hours): Cage climbs a ladder (or stands at a lectern, according to Weinrib) and reads a lecture riddled with long silences, perhaps excerpts from Meister Eckhart (disputed); Wolpe gets up and leaves in a fury; Cunningham dances in the aisles, chased by a little dog; Rauschenberg shows his paintings (black or white?) and winds up his phonograph for old records; M.C. Richards reads, Edna St. Vincent Millay from a ladder according to Weinrib, or she enters the room carried on a moving structure, a basket, or a “horse,” according to Litz; spectators take turns calling out the fragments of Olson's distributed poem; Tudor plays prepared piano, Water Music, and rattles; Jay Watt plays at the back on Lou Harrison's instruments; slides painted on glass and collages; perhaps a short film; at the end, coffee fills the cups, including those turned into ashtrays; two boys in white waltz together; faculty wives suck on Popsicles; Olson and Cage talk Zen again; Mrs. Jalowetz chants “Deep in the middle ages”. Words: Mrs. Jalowetz asks Cage where the best seat is, and Cage answers that they are all equally good. No one answers questions about the cups. Atmosphere: A three-ring circus; superimposed sounds (piano, records, voices, dogs, babies); for Litz, like a dream, with an unintelligible text in French; most spectators stay to the end, except Wolpe Stakes: Nothing less than the definition of a new theatrical form, and the conflict between aesthetic generations (Wolpe and Mrs. Jalowetz against Cage, Cunningham, and Tudor)

Kline stops in front of canvases on display and declares that they must be great paintings because he feels absolutely “helpless,” or “hopeless,” Cage no longer knows which. Words: Kline, as reported by Cage: sure they were great canvases because he felt absolutely “helpless/hopeless — in front of them” Atmosphere: grave admiration, a memory that “everyone thought marvelous”

After stopping the machine by dropping his knife into it, Rumaker has to jump into the silo to tramp down the silage blown in from the top; the corn keeps rising, for a man terrified of heights; he finally climbs down by the silo's metal rungs. Atmosphere: vertigo, rising silage, the blast of the fan Stakes: the poet's unfitness for physical labor

Setting off in the convertible with the top down as the moon rises; Olson drives fast, one big hand on the wheel, talking over his shoulder; Rumaker, deaf to his words in the wind, stays riveted on the immense golden moon against the black hills. Words: Olson talks easily and in a relaxed tone to his passengers Atmosphere: Wind in the ears, golden light, then an unearthly pale blue, enchantment Stakes: The applicant falls in love with the place and the master

Rumaker discovers the newborn asleep under mosquito netting in a basket, in the cool mountain air; he jokes about bears; Olson leans over and smiles: “My daughter... Still new to me”; the visitors tiptoe; Olson puts them at ease. Words: “Stolen by bears?” — “Outdoors is healthier for the child.”; “My daughter... Still new to me.”; “You don't need to creep about... Nothing wakes her. The most amazing thing.” Atmosphere: A cold night, luna moths at the windowpanes, the overhanging mountain rustling, fatherly tenderness Stakes: The tenderness beneath Olson's bulk revealed

Olson makes tea in the kitchen, chatting through the open door; he leafs through the poems at top speed and tosses them aside without a word; the story catches his attention: grunts, nods of the big head; he seriously declares his interest and advises him to apply; Rumaker admits his poverty; Olson explains the work scholarship; Mary Ann announces her refusal. Words: Olson: he should apply on the strength of the story and come see what he can learn there; later he will have to saturate himself in Dreiser Atmosphere: Cane chairs, tea, Olson in the midday of his nocturnal schedule Stakes: Rumaker's destiny turns: admission is possible

Olson proudly shows the poem “This,” printed by Nick Cernovich on orange paper with a sunflower/sun drawing; Rumaker understands nothing of it but nods to hide his naivete. Words: “Ain't it a smart job?” Atmosphere: The poet's fatherly pride, a craftsman's pride Stakes: Rumaker's initiation into the college's visual culture

A surprise arrival in midafternoon, during his father's shift at the shipyards; his mother apologizes for everything; Rumaker announces BMC; his mother, disconcerted, asks why 600 miles away; he quickly gathers his things and leaves before his father comes home. Words: “But why do you want to go to school 600 miles away?”, from his mother, who has never been farther than the other bank of the Delaware Atmosphere: Worn linoleum, a stifling closed room, cascading shame, haste Stakes: A silent break with his family, a farewell to childhood

Rumaker asks for Proust and Joyce; the librarian looks him over, takes out her big ring of keys, and leads him to the basement, chatting; he claims to be 21 (lying by a year); she unlocks the cabinet with the brown curtains. Words: She explains that these books are kept out of sight and must be asked for specially, and asks whether he is over 21. Atmosphere: A double sense of criminality, the memory of A Tree Grows in Brooklyn confiscated at age 12 Stakes: The future writer's initiatory transgression

Virginia takes a number of photographs at Black Mountain; this one taken, Rumaker stammers out his usual chatter; she rewinds her film, unruffled, and delivers her verdict Words: Virginia: “You exaggerate everything” Atmosphere: Flat, calm, babyish; the remark shuts Rumaker up Stakes: A writer's truth received from the most unlikely mouth

After lunch, Rumaker jabbers energetically; Virginia, rewinding her film behind her pale blue glasses, cuts him short with a remark; he falls silent, stung, then thinks it over alone in his study Words: Virginia, in a slow baby-talk voice: “You exaggerate everything” Atmosphere: After-lunch light, the photographer's unflappable calm against the young man's nervous flow Stakes: A lesson in truth that grounds Rumaker's ethic as a writer

Rumaker spends half an hour trying to work out what Madame means by the “noots” served at Natasha's Christmas dinner; she gets annoyed and shouts higher and higher until he understands “nuts” Words: Madame, shouting: “Noots! Noots!” Atmosphere: Comic misunderstanding, a rising elderly voice, dogs in the corner Stakes: The end of conversation in French; from now on the lesson is reduced to reading

Coming back from a movie in Asheville, they see a tall man in overalls with a baby in his arms; Joe stops, the man squeezes into the front next to Mary, says two words, and gets out stiffly at the college road Words: “Much obliged”; Mary afterward: there must be trouble at home. Atmosphere: Night on lonely roads, mute unease, unspoken rural distress Stakes: The mountain world briefly crosses the college's bubble

A work chain around the tractor and the conveyor; the farmers swap stories, gently mocking the “city slickers”; seeing the sun go down, Doyle speeds up the conveyor, and Rumaker runs out of breath cutting his twine (the accident follows, beyond the passage) Words: The farmers chuckle at sly observations about young city people discovering real work Atmosphere: Tongues as lazy as honey, corn dust, the sun going down toward the mountains, a pace gone frantic Stakes: The writer's body against the machine and the dusk

Rumaker sits on his bed; Dorothy murmurs her repeated phrases in a silky, seductive voice; rings of light dance before his eyes; on the verge of fainting he sits bolt upright and wakes, his hands and body trembling; Dorothy checks on him, calmly, laughs, and admits her first failure. Words: Dorothy, delighted: “But I almost gotcha!” Atmosphere: Drowsy, hypnotic, then nervous and reassuring; good-natured laughter. Stakes: Power, seduction, and resistance; the only failure of Dorothy's expertise.

Rumaker, needing to check his pancake makeup, has slipped away; Huss finds him in the restroom, tells him his entrance is long overdue, refuses his excuses, and hurries him back; Rumaker catches his breath, slips in through the side doors, and climbs back onto his platform under the gaze of the cast Words: Huss, evenly: everyone is waiting; is he sick? And he should save his excuses for later Atmosphere: Mute panic, a run down the stairs and across the road, shame as he climbs onto the platform Stakes: The failing student facing the punctilious director

Coming in for dinner as the winter night falls, Rumaker hears three or four students playing Bach on recorders by the dark windows Atmosphere: A gentle lifting of the spirit, a depopulated campus, the double darkness of the lake Stakes: The fragile beauty of a winter of decline

After his dishes, Rumaker goes in to shower; the veteran, naked under the bare bulbs, is drying himself with a little smile; Rumaker stands frozen in the doorway, burned by the image (coppery red hair, a body of fire), dares not speak, and flees into a stall Words: A mad, unspoken impulse: to offer himself for free, thinking of the gas money the man would save Atmosphere: Dazzling heat, hot water felt as coolness, paralyzing desire Stakes: The first explicit homosexual desire at the college, unconsummated

A day of torrential coastal rain: no one can go to the beach, no one reads or watches television; Elaine invites everyone to watch her paint Leo's portrait; everyone kibitzes and comments; she finishes a rather good picture Words: Elaine: “everyone there was some kind of expert, some kind of kibitzer” Atmosphere: Pouring rain, forced intimacy, chatter, Elaine serene in her element Stakes: Showing Elaine painting in public, claiming her place as an artist in a man's world

A cocktails-and-dinner party; Harold dominates the conversation; Jackson, depressed and already drunk, interrupts him with exclamations; Harold ignores him, then scorns him, tells him he has had enough to drink, and sends him to bed; Jackson docilely obeys; Lee explodes with rage Words: Pollock: “What a lot of shit”, “horse piss” Atmosphere: Mounting tension, public humiliation, contained rage, then an explosion Stakes: The birth of the public Pollock-de Kooning war, according to Naifeh and Smith
